01.r: The master answers the slave who hid his mina.
01.n: A present tense in a past narrative, which makes the moment vivid; this study keeps it, 'says'.

03.r: To the slave who did nothing with the money.

04.r: The judgment will come from the slave's own words.

05.r: With 'your', marks the slave's own mouth.
05.n: Greek says 'the mouth of you'; English uses 'your' alone.

06.r: What the slave has just said, standing for his words.
06.n: The BSB turns the picture into its meaning, 'by your own words'. Five translations keep 'mouth'.

07.r: The slave's own mouth, not anyone else's testimony.
07.n: The Greek has only 'of you'; the 'own' in five translations is English emphasis.

08.r: The master will give his verdict on the slave.
08.n: A future tense. The DRC's 'I judge' is a present.

10.r: The master's verdict on the slave's conduct.
10.n: Abbott-Smith derives it from πονέω, to toil, and records an early sense, 'oppressed by toils', before 'bad, worthless'. Here it is a moral charge.

11.r: Addressed as what he is: his master's property and agent.
11.n: Rendered 'slave' by this study's register, as in Luke 19:13; the translations say 'servant'.

12.r: The master takes up the slave's own claim to know him.
12.n: A pluperfect of the verb 'know'; Abbott-Smith notes that this verb's perfect has a present meaning and its pluperfect serves as an imperfect, so 'you knew'. The BSB reads the sentence as a question, 'So you knew ...?'; the Greek has no word that marks one, so the choice is the editor's.

14.n: The pronoun is written out, which the verb does not need. Abbott-Smith says the written pronoun is usually emphatic, though often with no apparent emphasis.

15.r: A generic word for a human being, here the master.

16.r: The slave's charge against the master, now repeated back to him: demanding and exacting.
16.n: Abbott-Smith gives its root sense as 'stringent, harsh to the taste', and its use of character as 'strict, severe'; English 'austere' comes from it. He lists σκληρός as a synonym, the word Matthew 25:24 uses ('hard'); this study keeps the two apart.

17.r: States his character as a present fact.
17.n: A present tense. The KJV and DRC put it in the past, 'was', to match 'knewest'.

18.r: Taking for himself what someone else put down.
18.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to raise, take up', and a later one 'to take away, carry off'. The BSB's 'withdrawing what I did not deposit' reads the pair of verbs as banking language, which is one reasonable reading of the picture.

21.r: The master takes what he did not set down himself.
21.n: Abbott-Smith's first sense is 'to place, lay, set'.

22.r: Joins the second half of the charge.

23.r: Present participle: a man who habitually reaps.
23.n: Abbott-Smith lists this verse among the figurative uses of the verb.

26.r: The master takes a crop he did not plant.

tr_note: The Textus Receptus adds δέ, 'and' or 'then', after the opening verb. The KJV's 'And he saith' and the Geneva's 'Then he sayde' show it; our text begins simply 'He says'.
